title: Spirituality and the Charles Lloyd Quartet in Antibes and Sweden
summary: McBee describes the quartet's first European performance after Duke Ellington and Ella Fitzgerald, the Golden Circle crowd, and how the church shaped his feeling in music.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: This is sort of a personal question, do you feel you are a spiritual man? Does faith play a significant role in your life?
So when you played with Alice Coltrane and Pharoah Sanders did you feel comfortable with the intent, the seeming intent of the music?

Well I’m not sure what I mean and I’m glad you asked that. It seems that the music had a reason for being other than just we have, you know we got a recording date, different from perhaps when a bop musician would get a date and they would get six or seven tunes together, some that they had written and some standards, where the music that you were involved in in the 60s seemed to have another level to it, that there was an intent to affect people as they listened.

Yes. That quality of expression for me began with the Charles Lloyd Quartet. It actually began, we were, I remember during our first performance in Antibes France, this is Jack DeJohnette, Keith Jarrett, myself and Charles Lloyd. We followed, we were fortunate to follow Duke Ellington featuring Ella Fitzgerald in Southern France right at the edge of the Mediterranean with maybe 3- 4,000 people seated outside sort of in an ampitheatrical set up there. We followed Duke Ellington featuring Ella Fitzgerald with the collective feeling that we’ve heard that. You know, we kind of discussed that in the dressing room but as they say, we wanted to get out and play, this was our first time in Europe playing, come on, let’s go, you’re playing too long. Now that we are on the stage the music was so exciting insofar as how we were feeling, the confidence in each other to express what we had experienced previous to our arrival in Europe. It was absolutely amazing. We felt so energized and so exciting about how we were feeling individually and collectively that would affect, that would seem to affect the audience. The audience were really very excited about our performance. So the performance, with the performance having been so successful, our next concert, which was at the Golden Circle in Sweden, was just overflowed by people that followed us from Southern France to that club to hear us, you know, we were excited to know that upon stepping on the stage people would just really demonstrate great excitement to see us walk on the concert stage, not only into the stage not only just to play. So we realized, personally I realized that we were expressing something that was rather intrinsical, because if you think of Keith Jarrett and Jack DeJohnette and myself, we all were people that felt something when we played. And here were three people — along with four people — along with Charles Lloyd that played music that had a quality of spirit with it. Matter of fact Heikki Sarmanto, a Finnish pianist that I met during that tour, we are good friends to today and he helps me out a lot about how the people felt who we were, you know. We weren’t just playing tunes we were feeling something. And so as I said before, I’m one who is intent to express when I play the instrument, whatever it is I’m there to express a quality of feeling that, you know,

would sometimes come from a place that I don’t even know about. When I was a young man of course there was the church and there was the community where you heard music that made you, that called your attention to persons or groups that were feeling something. So the Charles Lloyd group was one that prepared me for that Alice Coltrane recording, because that “Journey in Satchidananda” meant that she was going there to pray, to respect the gods of her choice, you know, so far as being her continued existence musically and personally. So I think over the years I’ve gotten a lot of fine comments about how I play, you just mentioned on that record, and it was about something that I felt. And to this day that’s who I am. When I play my instrument I’m very privileged to be quiet and play a couple of notes and I’m just fine.
